claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among the quinary alloy and its quaternary and ternary subsets arise from variations in local chemical short-range order.
Variations in local chemical short-range order produce differences in lattice-distortion magnitude.
The compared equiatomic alloys are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
The quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys should be compared using identical processing, testing conditions, and sample geometries.
Holding temperature, strain rate, and processing history constant isolates composition-related effects on deformation.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has greater local chemical order than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater local chemical order in the quinary alloy induces larger lattice distortions.
Greater local chemical order in the quinary alloy induces more spatially heterogeneous lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The proposed impediment to dislocation motion gives the quinary alloy a higher yield strength than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The proposed impediment to dislocation motion gives the quinary alloy greater strain hardening than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Nanoscale characterization by atom-probe tomography and high-resolution TEM can determine the relevant chemical order and local lattice distortions.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys that retain a single-phase FCC microstructure after identical thermomechanical processing.
Factors in addition to chemical short-range order may contribute to the mechanical-property differences.
The magnitude of the predicted effects is uncertain without multiscale testing.
Failure of the quinary alloy to exhibit significantly greater local chemical order and lattice distortion would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of the quinary alloy to exhibit superior yield strength and strain hardening would falsify the hypothesis.
